news.title: Advancing computer-use agents for healthcare teams
news.source_text:
Advancing computer-use agents for healthcare teams
Healthcare is fragmented, and teams often need to move information between systems manually before a patient can get care. When a clinician recommends an MRI, for example, the information an insurer needs may be in a patient’s medical record, but a team member still needs to retrieve it and enter it into a separate portal to complete an authorization request.
Computer-use agents carry out multi-step workflows by clicking, typing, and moving between applications. In healthcare, this enables AI to help with repetitive workflows in the software teams already use.
Today, we’re sharing new results measuring model performance, safety, and cost in clinical and administrative workflows. We’re also sharing the ways we’re working with leading healthcare organizations like Abridge, Ambience, Cigna Healthcare, and CVS Health to advance and apply computer use, across authorization requests, referrals, discharge planning, and outreach between visits.
Healthcare teams, developers, and individual clinicians can access these capabilities today through the OpenAI API, ChatGPT for Healthcare, and ChatGPT for Clinicians. Organizations can support HIPAA-compliant workflows, configure approvals and agent access, and record audit logs for secure deployments.
To show how a computer-use agent can help a clinician and an authorization specialist work on the same MRI request, we built a demo using synthetic patient data. A patient messages their clinician about lower back pain. A computer-use agent reviews the patient’s visit notes, physical therapy records, and prior imaging in the EHR. It drafts an MRI order, an encounter note, and a reply to the patient for the clinician to review. The agent then uses the same records to prepare a prior authorization request in the insurer’s portal for an authorization specialist to review.
We evaluated GPT‑6 Astra on tasks clinicians handle in their EHR inboxes. These tasks, shaped by physician input, require Astra to carry out multi-step workflows designed to test both clinical reasoning over longitudinal patient context and navigation of complex interfaces. Reviewers examined the model’s actions alongside the notes, orders, and patient messages it produced, assessing whether the work would be helpful and clinically safe in the context of the task.
Clinical safety was assessed by evaluating whether inaccuracies, omissions, or actions in the model’s work could plausibly lead to patient harm. Overall, 99% of 325 reviewed tasks were rated safe. Physicians rated helpfulness on a five-point scale, selecting “very helpful” or “extremely helpful” in 93% of 646 assessments.
We also evaluated computer-use agents for administrative tasks, such as prior authorizations, appeals, and medical equipment orders. On HealthAdminBench(opens in a new window), an independent benchmark from Stanford researchers measuring performance on common administrative workflows, GPT‑6 Astra earned 94.3% of available
news.summary: OpenAI introduces GPT‑6 Astra computer-use agents that automate multi-step healthcare workflows, such as prior authorizations and discharge planning, through the OpenAI API and ChatGPT for Clinicians. These agents can navigate multiple applications, draft clinical orders, and log audit trails while maintaining HIPAA compliance.
news.enterprise_use: S1: Review OpenAI’s GPT‑6 Astra API documentation and test the agent in a sandbox environment to see if it can automate routine administrative tasks in your organization’s existing EHR and insurer portals. S2: Not integrating these agents could mean continued manual data entry, increasing staff workload and error risk. S3: Your IT stack—particularly JumpCloud for identity, Google Workspace for collaboration, and Freshservice for ticketing—can be leveraged to orchestrate and monitor these agent-driven workflows.

news.title: LVMH’s Media Division announces strategic partnership with OpenAI
news.summary_raw: LVMH’s Media Division and OpenAI announce a partnership to support journalism with AI and make its publications more accessible through ChatGPT.
news.source_text:
LVMH’s Media Division announces strategic partnership with OpenAI
This news was originally shared by LVMH’s Media Division and can be read here(opens in a new window).
Paris, 16 November 2026—LVMH Group’s Media Division and OpenAI announce the signing of a strategic agreement to support new uses of artificial intelligence across all the division’s publications and make their journalism more accessible through ChatGPT. The agreement includes the deployment of OpenAI tools and ChatGPT Enterprise to teams across the media division, enabling them to develop AI applications tailored to their day-to-day work.
Their shared ambition is to empower teams across the media division to experiment with and develop practical uses of AI that support journalism and high-quality reporting.
Artificial intelligence is a powerful tool that, when put to work in newsrooms, enables journalists to focus on the core of their profession: investigating, analysing and writing. Teams will be able to explore applications such as document research, document comparison and preliminary translation. The goal is to enable them to devote more time to investigative reporting, analysis and reporting in the field.
In addition, in an increasingly crowded information landscape, personalisation has become a major priority. Artificial intelligence is an essential tool for developing and delivering products and services that meet the needs of customers, readers and advertisers alike, helping to attract and retain them and grow revenue across the publications.
This partnership is a company-wide initiative that also enhances the presence of content from LVMH Group’s Media Division in ChatGPT, providing summaries and excerpts in response to relevant user questions, identifying their sources and including direct links to the original articles. The partnership will extend across all the division’s publications and support the evolution of roles throughout the organisation: streamlining operations, improving efficiency, and encouraging innovation and creativity to prepare today’s publications for tomorrow. The rollout will be supported by training tailored to everyone’s use cases.
About LVMH Group’s Media Division
LVMH Group’s media division, Groupe Les Echos-Le Parisien, brings together 17 media brands covering news, finance, culture, heritage, arts and music. With 1,800 employees, including nearly 700 journalists, it reaches more than 27 million people in France every month.
The Group’s media brands: Boursier.com(opens in a new window), Capital Finance, Challenges, Connaissance des Arts, Historia, Investir, La Lettre de l’Expansion, L’Agefi, Le Parisien, Aujourd’hui en France, Les Echos, L’Opinion, medici.tv(opens in a new window), Mezzo, Mieux Vivre Votre Argent, Paris Match, Radio Classique.
The Group’s exhibitions and publishing houses: Citadelles & Mazenod, Fine Arts Paris, In Fine, Salon du Dessin.
news.summary: LVMH’s Media Division has signed a strategic partnership with OpenAI to deploy ChatGPT Enterprise across its publications, enabling AI‑driven journalism tools such as document research, comparison, and translation. The collaboration aims to boost content accessibility, personalization, and operational efficiency within LVMH’s media brands.
news.enterprise_use: Keep an eye on how LVMH integrates ChatGPT Enterprise into their workflows; it may set a precedent for AI‑driven content operations that could influence best practices for managing large document repositories and content personalization in enterprise environments.

news.source_text:
The Secret Thinkpad Powerbutton Code To Bring Dead Laptops Back To Life
Two months ago, I got a new laptop. It’s a Lenovo Thinkpad z61t. I actually ordered a t61, but I accidentally got the z61 instead — and, I actually really like it. It’s quite similar to the t61, but a little smaller and lighter. I was worried that the smaller part would be a problem, but I’ve gotten used to it. I really like the fact that it’s much lighter than my old t42. It just makes it seem so much more usable on the go. Lugging out the t42 was always a chore.
Anyway, I was at the Office 2.0 conference today, where I was giving a little presentation on the Techdirt Insight Community, and about an hour before the presentation, I went to find a quiet place to practice the presentation… and discovered that my brand new laptop wouldn’t work. I knew something was wrong when the “sleep” light wasn’t lit. I started to get worried when I plugged in the laptop and the battery light didn’t light up. Then I noticed that even though the machine had been asleep, it was really really hot. Pushing the power button did nothing. No lights were on and nothing seemed to get them to turn on. I pulled out the battery and put it back in and that did nothing as well.
So I called up IBM support and explained the situation. The guy on the other end then let me in on the secret power button code to revive your dead Thinkpad. After assessing the situation (totally dead laptop) he warned me: “Okay, this is going to sound totally bizarre, but I want you to give this a try…” He then had me unplug the AC adapter and take out the battery. Then, you push the power button 10 times in a row at one second intervals. Next, you push and hold the power button for 30 seconds. Then you put the battery back in and push the power button… and she lives. The computer came back, good as ever.
I asked the guy what the power button pushing incantation did and he said “static discharge” so apparently there was some sort of static that caused a short or something. I tried to get the guy to explain in more detail what happened, but he said “dude, you know as much as I do… but your machine is working.”
And so it is.
So, if you happen to have a Thinkpad that suddenly drops completely dead for no reason, try the power button trick.
Forget up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right, B, A. This little code is now the coolest “cheat” code I know…
